prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, enabling atomic frequency standards with fractional uncertainty at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement advance in the plainest sense: magic-wavelength trapping removes the Stark and motional shifts that limited earlier neutral-atom clocks while keeping the statistical power of thousands of atoms, taking fractional uncertainty from the 1e-16 range of the best earlier standards to about 1e-18. The result is not a single record in one laboratory. It has been reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, including fibre-linked clock comparisons, so the reproducibility question I always ask is answered. It has real downstream use: relativistic geodesy at centimetre height resolution, laboratory tests of constants and dark-sector models, and the working basis for the coming redefinition of the second. Katori (the 2001-2003 proposal and first Sr lattice clocks) and Ye (accuracy, stability and the many-body clock) have separable, well documented contributions, so a two-person prize is clean. The ballot list is also the only one where all eight members independently name the same two laureates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes. Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control and ion clocks) already cover the comb and the single-ion clock, and a sceptic can say that a lattice clock is an application of recognised tools. I do not think that holds, because the magic-wavelength idea is a separate concept and the many-atom statistical gain is something ion clocks cannot offer. It does mean the citation must be written carefully around the lattice concept and not around clocks or combs in general. A second reservation is timing: the redefinition of the second is pending, so one can argue for waiting. Against this, a Nobel Prize recognises the discovery and demonstrated performance, not the metrological decision. Credit is also a question, since Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto and others did much of the hands-on work, and two names will leave some of them out.

responses.point: She ranks B013 first alongside me, citing Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstration of 10^-18 systematic uncertainty as a clean two-person configuration, with independent confirmation by several laboratories.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the pairing. I would add one qualification to her framing. Atomic structure knowledge matters less here than the metrological discipline: the 10^-18 claim rests on carefully characterised blackbody-radiation shifts, lattice light shifts and density shifts, and those evaluations were checked by clock comparisons between laboratories, not by one group's own budget. That comparison record is the real evidence of maturity, and I think the citation and the committee text should lean on it. I also take her point that the 2012 prize overlaps in context, but it covered ion trapping and cavity QED, which is a different route.

responses.point: He places B035 (IceCube) first as an instrument-led discovery that opened a new observational window, with B013 second, and notes that the credit for IceCube is not clean because a large collaboration built it.
responses.response: I respect the instrument-led argument and I weigh new ways of observing nature heavily myself. But the attribution difficulty he raises is exactly why I rank B013 higher. B013 has two clearly separable originators, while for IceCube the committee would be choosing among Halzen, Spiering, and collaboration and DUMAND/AMANDA leaders. The astrophysical source evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is also still a few objects at a few sigma, whereas the clock performance is reproduced across many labs. I would not call B035 immature, but it is less settled, and I would keep it as an alternative for a later year.

responses.point: He ranks B034 (Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase) first as a unifying concept with enormous cross-field reach, arguably overdue, and ranks B013 only sixth.
responses.response: I accept that geometric phases are a deep unifying idea and that Berry-phase measurements are well confirmed. I disagree on priority. The priority issues he flags himself (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam, Mead-Truhlar, Simon) make a clean attribution to two people harder, and age alone should not decide it. B013 also gives us a discovery that is still producing new measurements and tools. I do not want to treat an overdue discovery as automatically ahead of a recent measurement advance. His B013 ranking of sixth looks low to me given his own note that Katori and Ye are the natural pair and the precision is orders of magnitude beyond caesium.

responses.point: He ranks B008 (circuit QED) first as the architecture underlying essentially all superconducting quantum processors, with a very mature record.
responses.response: I rank B008 fifth, so I take it seriously as a methods advance. My reservations are two. First, the decisive first strong-coupling experiment was by Wallraff with Schoelkopf's group, and Wallraff is not in the credited names, so the triple of Blais, Schoelkopf and Girvin does not follow the original experimental work. Second, the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes another superconducting-circuit award soon more awkward. If the committee wanted B008 it would need to work out the attribution first.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (ion control) prizes, which depends on how the citation is worded.
Whether hands-on contributors to the 10^-18 evaluations (Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto and others) change the view that two laureates suffice.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing, and whether the committee prefers to wait for it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B013, B001 or B035. As a Lund atomic physicist I know the optical clock and cold-atom communities, and my profile shows a distant Boulder connection through a PhD-period stay in John Hall's lab, but Hall is not a candidate here and Katori and Ye are not named as collaborators. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Johansson's Chalmers home, which matters only for discussion of B008, where I rank it fifth.
